claim: A viral video shows a police officer arresting a young child for fishing.
label: False
ruling: False: Cumbria Police said the clip shows officers responding to a report of a child with a knife, the encounter had no connection to fishing, and no knife was found and no arrests were made.

claim: On 22 May 2025, Cumbria Police officers responded to a report of a child in possession of a knife in public; boys were handcuffed while being searched, no knife was found and no arrest was made.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: 100 years ago the UK had no income tax, no beer or tobacco levies, no inheritance tax and no national debt.
label: False
ruling: Full Fact found the claim wrong: income tax, beer and tobacco levies and a precursor to inheritance tax all existed in the UK over 100 years ago, and the UK had a large national debt at the time.

claim: The UK's national debt stood at £7,738 million at the end of 1925, and UK income tax, first introduced in 1799, has been in force every year since 1842.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Airlines, including airlines in Spain and Russia, are banning Covid-vaccinated people from flying because of the risk of fatal blood clots on high-altitude flights.
label: False
ruling: Full Fact rated this false, finding no evidence that any airline is banning vaccinated people from flying or has considered doing so, and no evidence that any Covid vaccine raises the risk of DVT while flying.

claim: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a condition in which a blood clot forms in a vein, usually in the leg, and it can occur during long journeys of over four hours, including by plane.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Henry Kissinger gave a speech to the World Health Organisation "Council on Eugenics" on 25 February 2009 on eugenics and mandatory forcible vaccinations, saying that vaccine-makers stand to make millions as "the herd pays us for providing extermination services".
label: False
ruling: Full Fact rated this false: there is no record of Kissinger making such a speech, the WHO says the "Council on Eugenics" does not exist, and his representatives called the claim a complete fabrication.

claim: Henry Kissinger, a former US Secretary of State, died in 2023.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: The ethylene oxide used to sterilise cervical smear test swabs is cancer-causing, making smear tests dangerous for patients.
label: Misleading
ruling: Full Fact rated the claim as missing context: ethylene oxide can be carcinogenic at higher, prolonged exposure, but there is no credible evidence it endangers patients who come into contact with sterilised medical devices, so the implied claim that smear tests are unsafe is false.

claim: Ethylene oxide is a gas commonly used to sterilise medical devices, including swabs and speculums.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Europe's record-breaking June 2026 heatwave was caused by El Niño, not climate change.
label: False
ruling: False: climate scientists have shown the high temperatures Western Europe experienced in the heatwave would have been impossible without climate change, and El Niño is a natural cycle playing out atop human-caused warming, not a replacement for it.

claim: The 11 years from 2015 to 2025 were the 11 hottest years on record.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Sunscreen is harmful to human health and causes cancer.
label: False
ruling: Science Feedback found that published studies do not show sunscreen causes cancer or harms health; sunscreen chemicals can enter the body, but harmful effects have not been demonstrated, and correlations with skin cancer reflect the sunscreen paradox of longer sun exposure.

claim: Ultraviolet radiation, which is contained in sunlight, is recognized as a cancer-causing agent by the International Agency for Research on Cancer.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Mainstream medicine ignores natural remedies and naturally occurring therapeutic compounds.
label: False
ruling: Science Feedback rules this false: drug development often draws on natural compounds, producing mainstream medicines such as penicillin, aspirin, paclitaxel, artemisinin and ivermectin.

claim: The anticancer chemotherapy drug paclitaxel is derived from the Pacific yew tree.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: The taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Donald Trump that began airing in September 2026 are public service announcements comparable to those paid for by past presidential administrations of both parties, including the George W. Bush, Obama and Biden administrations.
label: Misleading
ruling: Misleading: experts consulted saw no real comparison, as the cited past examples were largely informational campaigns such as Affordable Care Act enrollment and COVID-19 vaccination ads, one Obama-era example was found illegal by the GAO, and the Trump ads appear more political.

claim: In December 2015, the Government Accountability Office concluded that the Environmental Protection Agency had violated federal laws through a social media outreach campaign supporting its proposed clean water rule, finding it engaged in covert propaganda and grassroots lobbying.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Troy Jackson, the Democratic candidate in Maine's U.S. Senate race, wants to raise Social Security taxes, hurting seniors.
label: Misleading
ruling: FactCheck.org found the claim misleading: Jackson proposes eliminating the cap on earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax, which would affect high earners still working, not raise the tax rate or tax benefits, and current beneficiaries are unlikely to be affected.

claim: The maximum amount of annual earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax is $184,500 for 2026.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan voted to raise Alaskans' healthcare costs by $1,800 and on that same day voted to give himself a $500,000 taxpayer-funded payout.
label: Misleading
ruling: FactCheck.org found the WinSenate ad misleading: Sullivan's November 2025 vote for the shutdown-ending bill omitted an extension of ACA subsidies and included a provision allowing senators to sue for $500,000, but he later voted to extend the subsidies, only 3.2% of Alaskans are on ACA plans, and he never sought or received any payout and voted to repeal the provision.

claim: The Senate passed the funding bill to end the government shutdown 60-40 on Nov. 10, 2025, and a later appropriations bill signed into law repealed its provision allowing senators whose phone toll records were obtained without proper notification to sue the federal government for $500,000 or actual damages.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska, took money from liberals who opened U.S. borders to drug cartels and voted with them against securing the border.
label: Misleading
ruling: FactCheck.org found the claim misleading and missing context: Peltola voted against the 2023 Secure the Border Act but backed a nearly identical bill in 2024 and often broke with her party on border issues, and most fentanyl enters through legal ports of entry, mostly carried by U.S. citizens.

claim: Mary Peltola was one of five Democrats who voted for the End the Border Catastrophe Act in the U.S. House on April 20, 2024.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of Ohio, has lied about her difficult childhood, and her account of growing up living in a tent is not true.
label: Mostly false
ruling: FactCheck.org found that court records, contemporaneous news reports, a police report and her brother's statements corroborate key elements of Acton's account, undercutting the Ramaswamy campaign ad's claim that she lied about her past.

claim: Cledith Arthur, the stepfather of Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, was charged with rape in July 1978 and indicted by a grand jury that September.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Data centers coming online are almost always accompanied by a multiyear freeze in electricity prices, making them a massive force to reduce the price of electricity and stop price rises.
label: Misleading
ruling: Misleading: data centers can lower prices in some places, particularly where grids have spare capacity, but the effect depends on local conditions, and data including from the Energy Department's own lab show they have contributed to price increases in areas such as the PJM region.

claim: National average retail electricity prices in the United States rose 29% between 2019 and 2025, or 3% when adjusted for inflation, according to a report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the Brattle Group.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: President Donald Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act gutted Medicare by making huge cuts to the program.
label: Misleading
ruling: Misleading: the law's Medicare changes are narrow and affect relatively few beneficiaries, its big health cuts fall on Medicaid, and the larger automatic PAYGO Medicare cuts it could have triggered were waived by Congress.

claim: The November 2025 law that reopened the U.S. government after a six-week shutdown eliminated any Statutory Pay-As-You-Go spending cuts that would have been triggered by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Sen. Susan Collins voted to cover up the Epstein files and received $3 million to her super PAC from Jeffrey Epstein's business partner.
label: Misleading
ruling: FactCheck.org found the WinSenate ads misleading: Collins voted to table an amendment to a defense bill but the Senate, without her opposition, later passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and the $3 million donor, Stephen Schwarzman, was merely a fellow founding member of a private club, which makes "business partner" a stretch.

claim: The Epstein Files Transparency Act passed the U.S. Senate by unanimous consent in November 2025.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Touchscreen voting machines in the United States are deliberately changing Democratic votes to Republican votes in the 2026 elections.
label: False
ruling: False: there is no evidence that machines are deliberately switching votes; experts and election officials attribute the reported problems to familiar touchscreen calibration issues or voter error, and nearly all voters can review a paper ballot before their votes are cast.

claim: According to Verified Voting, only 1.3% of U.S. registered voters, those living in Louisiana, use electronic voting machines that record votes without the voter ever seeing a paper ballot.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Democratic candidates James Talarico, Roy Cooper, Chris Pappas and Bob Brooks oppose the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's tax cuts on tips, overtime and Social Security and back higher taxes on them.
label: Misleading
ruling: FactCheck.org found the attack ads misleading: opposing the OBBBA overall does not equal opposing these provisions, and the candidates say they support the tax cuts on tips, overtime and Social Security, objecting instead to benefits for the wealthy and cuts to Medicaid and food aid.

claim: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law by President Donald Trump on July 4, 2025, includes tax deductions related to tips, overtime pay and people age 65 and older that expire after 2028.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Chris Pappas's net worth has risen by upwards of 1,000% while in Congress, going from as low as negative $669,974 in 2018 to over $6 million in 2025.
label: False
ruling: False: FactCheck.org found the 1,000% figure comes only from cherry-picking opposite ends of the disclosure ranges, and his disclosures show a much more modest increase, mostly due to listing his husband's assets on more recent forms.

claim: Chris Pappas's 2025 congressional financial disclosure lists assets worth about $1.8 million to $7.1 million and liabilities of about $1 million to $2.2 million, while his 2018 disclosure lists assets of around $1.3 million to $6 million and liabilities of about $900,000 to $2 million.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: James Talarico voted for an income tax in Texas.
label: False
ruling: False: FactCheck.org found Talarico never voted for an income tax; he opposed a 2019 joint resolution for a constitutional amendment prohibiting one, in a state that has no such tax and already restricted it, and he says he has always been against one.

claim: Texas does not have an individual income tax, and a constitutional amendment approved by voters in 2019 means that prohibition can only be changed with a two-thirds vote in the Legislature and approval by voters.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, wants to defund the police, has called for abolishing prisons, and has a plan to commute sentences for murderers and rapists.
label: Misleading
ruling: FactCheck.org found the Republican-aligned ads misleading: they omit context or exaggerate, since El-Sayed's 2020 "defund" remarks were about reallocating funds and he now backs investing in law enforcement, he never called for abolishing prisons, and the commutation proposal came from his 2018 governor campaign and covered people convicted as minors.

claim: Abdul El-Sayed's 2018 campaign plan for governor of Michigan proposed reviewing the sentences of all prisoners sentenced before age 18 with the aim of commuting sentences for those deemed low risk, with credit for time served.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Democratic Senate candidates Sherrod Brown of Ohio, James Talarico of Texas and Mary Peltola of Alaska support sex changes for minors, including taxpayer-funded sex change surgeries on children.
label: Misleading
ruling: FactCheck.org found the Republican ads flawed and misleading: they rely on Brown's general remark about a broader bill and on votes by Talarico and Peltola against measures that went beyond surgeries or were opposed for other reasons, and Talarico says he opposes such surgeries for minors.

claim: Ohio enacted a law in 2024 prohibiting gender-affirming medication and surgery for minors, with exceptions for children with sex development disorders, after the Ohio Legislature overrode Gov. Mike DeWine's veto.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Crystal Mason was sentenced to five years in prison for illegal voting because of Ken Paxton's crackdown on voters of color.
label: Misleading
ruling: FactCheck.org found the Talarico ad misleading and missing context: Mason's case was investigated and prosecuted by the Tarrant County District Attorney's Office, not Paxton's office, and the judge gave no explanation for the sentence, so it is unclear whether Paxton's efforts influenced it.

claim: The illegal voting case against Crystal Mason, who was charged in February 2017, was investigated and prosecuted by the Tarrant County District Attorney's Office in Texas.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, was hospitalized as a patient at the Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health facility in Mason, Ohio, in October 2026.
label: False
ruling: False: the Lindner Center of Hope said Talarico has never received treatment there, and he was recovering from the flu at his Austin, Texas, home, as confirmed by New York Times review of time-stamped security camera images.

claim: Ken Paxton, the Texas Attorney General, is the Republican candidate opposing James Talarico in the 2026 U.S. Senate race in Texas.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: At an Oct. 5, 2026 rally in Nebraska, President Donald Trump advocated for Iran to attack Los Angeles and San Diego, saying foreign enemies should "take out" the two cities.
label: Misleading
ruling: FactCheck.org found this reading misleading: though Trump's wording was confusing, the context, his past comments and the White House's clarification indicate he meant the war would stop Iran from threatening U.S. cities and that higher gas prices are a small price to pay.

claim: In March 2025, the U.S. Intelligence Community said that "Iran is not building a nuclear weapon."
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: The Biden administration's 2024 power plant carbon emissions regulations threatened the reliability of the U.S. electrical grid, and repealing them was needed to ensure Americans have dependable electricity.
label: Misleading
ruling: FactCheck.org found Trump administration officials misleadingly cast the Biden-era power plant rule as a threat to grid reliability, with experts calling the notion unfounded because the rule required no abrupt transition and grid operators were not seeking the deregulation.

claim: During the 2021 Winter Storm Uri in Texas, natural gas was by far the largest contributor to power outages, followed by wind and then coal.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: The Trump administration's most favored nation drug-pricing deals with pharmaceutical companies will save Medicaid more than $64 billion and are rescuing state budgets.
label: Misleading
ruling: Exaggerated: the $64 billion figure is an uncertain 10-year White House projection that depends on undisclosed deal terms and which drugs and states participate, outside estimates are lower, and even the projected savings to states would initially be under 2% of their annual Medicaid spending and would diminish over time.

claim: In fiscal year 2024, Medicaid's gross spending on prescription drugs topped $106 billion, while net spending after rebates was $48 billion, according to the Medicaid and CHIP Payment and Access Commission.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall voted to keep the Epstein files sealed, helping cover up Jeffrey Epstein's crimes and protecting pedophiles.
label: Misleading
ruling: Misleading: Marshall voted against a September 2025 Democratic amendment to release the Epstein files, saying he opposed attaching it to an unrelated defense bill, but he supported the standalone law compelling their release two months later.

claim: A standalone bill requiring the U.S. Justice Department to publicly release the Epstein files cleared the Senate by unanimous consent and became law in November 2025.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Any U.S. election ballot that a poll worker writes on, including a letter, checkmark, star, or an R or D, will be disqualified.
label: False
ruling: Snopes rated the rumor false: election officials say a poll worker's marking does not disqualify a ballot, no state was found to disqualify ballots for markings unless the voter's selections are unreadable, and several states require poll workers to mark ballots.

claim: Election laws in Minnesota, Missouri and Texas require poll workers to mark ballots.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: U.S. Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina said she did not want to be a senator and that, "When I get to heaven one day, I am just going to choke Lindsey."
label: Contested
ruling: Mixture: Graham did say in an Oct. 28 radio interview that she would choke Lindsey when she gets to heaven, but there is no evidence she ever said she did not want to be a senator, and she reportedly said she loves the job.

claim: Darline Graham, who filled the U.S. Senate seat left vacant by the death of her brother Lindsey Graham, faced Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina's 2026 Senate race.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: In October 2026, the U.S. Army trained soldiers to dig mass battlefield graves for American troops as the U.S. war on Iran continued.
label: True
ruling: True: the images and the claim were real, as Defense Department-distributed photos and an Army report document an Oct. 21, 2026, exercise practicing temporary interment trenches, although it was unclear what specifically the exercise was preparing for, and conclusions about an imminent threat appear to have originated on social media rather than with the Army.

claim: Phase II of Operation Dragon Covenant, a test-of-concept exercise executed by the U.S. Army's 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, took place near the St. Mere Eglise Drop Zone in October 2026.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Patrick Stewart said in 2017 of Donald Trump: "The fact is, when America sneezes, the world catches a cold. America, I think, is on the edge of a very bad flu infection, and it's because of the man who is in the White House."
label: True
ruling: True: Snopes found the quote is correctly attributed to Stewart, who made the remark in a video interview with The A.V. Club published on Nov. 16, 2017.

claim: Patrick Stewart was knighted in 2010 for his services to drama.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Vivek Ramaswamy was booed off stage in Ohio after telling the crowd, "The truth of the matter is, people in my generation have already made it. We're gonna be fine."
label: Contested
ruling: Mixture: the speech was real and Ramaswamy was booed throughout, but it took place on July 29, 2026, he was misquoted, the viral clip was edited to compress events, he kept speaking for over a minute after the remark, and whether he cut his speech short could not be determined.

claim: Vivek Ramaswamy was billed as the keynote speaker at the Young Americans for Liberty convention held in Cleveland, Ohio, where he spoke on July 29, 2026.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said authorities would "look into Abdul El-Sayed's immigration status and see if he committed fraud."
label: False
ruling: Snopes found no evidence Rubio made the statement, concluding the quote was incorrectly attributed to him and appeared to originate from a Facebook page that described some of its content as satire.

claim: Abdul El-Sayed was born in Rochester Hills, Michigan, on Oct. 31, 1984.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar married her brother, Ahmed Elmi, to commit immigration fraud.
label: Unproven
ruling: Snopes left the claim unrated, finding it unfounded for now because the evidence of family ties between Omar and Elmi is circumstantial, relies on similar names and ignores Somali naming conventions, and no DNA proof exists.

claim: Minnesota court records show that the marriage of Ilhan Omar and Ahmed Nur Said Elmi was legally dissolved on Dec. 4, 2017.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Fraudsters in U.S. elections are skewing results by having individual voters receive multiple ballots and vote more than once.
label: Unproven
ruling: Snopes left the claim unrated, finding no documented proof of multiple ballots per voter being used to cast multiple votes on a scale that could skew results, and noting that extra ballots are usually mistakes and that safeguards limit each voter to one vote.

claim: A vendor error caused 7,791 voters in Tulare County, California, to be sent an extra vote-by-mail ballot for the Nov. 3, 2026, midterm election.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Staffers for Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola engaged in ballot-stacking by recruiting a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to run in the 2026 Senate race to confuse voters and draw votes away from Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
label: Unproven
ruling: Snopes found no reason to doubt The New York Times' reporting on the alleged ballot-stacking plan, but could not view the evidence or independently confirm it, so the claim remains unconfirmed; the Peltola campaign denies involvement.

claim: On June 26, 2026, the Alaska Supreme Court permitted Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, to appear on the ballot for Alaska's U.S. Senate election after the Alaska Division of Elections had moved to remove him.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: The $5 million gold covering of the recently regilded equestrian statues in Washington, D.C., was melting off in late October 2026.
label: Unproven
ruling: Snopes left the claim unrated and still under investigation because it could not directly confirm that the streaks meant the gilding was melting off, while the National Park Service said they came from moisture draining and did not indicate damage to the gilding.

claim: On April 21, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Interior awarded $5.1 million to The Gilder's Studio, a company in Maryland, for the full conservation and regilding of four monumental equestrian bronze sculptures.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: Emergency preparedness guidelines released by multiple countries in and around October 2026 are a sign that a catastrophic, life-changing event is about to happen.
label: False
ruling: Snopes found the claim unfounded: countries including the U.K., U.S. and Japan did release new preparedness campaigns in 2026, but such guidance is long-standing routine, many European countries were following a 2025 EU strategy, and none of it shows a catastrophe is imminent.

claim: The European Union released a new emergency preparedness strategy in March 2025.
label: True
ruling: established by the article

claim: U.S. President Donald Trump sexually abused New York psychologist Dr. Larissa Portnoff when she was a minor, starting when she was around 8 years old.
label: Unproven
ruling: Snopes said it could not rate the allegation true or false because it could not be independently verified, was originally made anonymously, is not public record and has not been tried in court, while the White House categorically denied it.

claim: Donald Trump bought the Miss Universe organization, which included the Miss Teen USA pageant, in 1996 and part-owned it with NBC until 2015.
label: True
ruling: established by the article
